toc.title: Advantages of a Strong Definition of Done (CSM 1.15)
How the Definition of Done Evolves (SF 4.8)
Multiple Teams, One Definition of Done (SF 4.9)
Exam Traps and What the Exam Expects

html:
1The Increment (SF 4.1)

"An Increment is a concrete stepping stone toward the Product Goal. Each Increment is additive to all prior Increments and thoroughly verified, ensuring that all Increments work together. In order to provide value, the Increment must be usable."

Attribute (list at least three) Meaning
A step toward the Product Goal Every Increment moves the product closer to the goal
Additive It adds to all prior Increments; they accumulate into the product
Thoroughly verified Checked so that all Increments work together
Usable It must be usable to provide value
Meets the Definition of Done "Work cannot be considered part of an Increment unless it meets the Definition of Done"
Inspectable The sum of the Increments is presented at the Sprint Review, "thus supporting empiricism"

"The moment a Product Backlog item meets the Definition of Done, an Increment is born."

1.1 Multiple Increments in a Sprint (SF 4.5)

"Multiple Increments may be created within a Sprint. The sum of the Increments is presented at the Sprint Review thus supporting empiricism. However, an Increment may be delivered to stakeholders prior to the end of the Sprint. The Sprint Review should never be considered a gate to releasing value."

How it works: each time an item meets the Definition of Done, a new Increment exists and is added to the earlier ones. A team that finishes items throughout the Sprint therefore has several Increments, not one "big bang" at the end. Stakeholders may receive them as soon as they are usable.

Old wording

The 2017 Guide said the Increment is "a body of inspectable, done work that supports empiricism at the end of the Sprint", must be "in useable condition regardless of whether the Product Owner decides to release it", and spoke of "potentially releasable" functionality. The 2020 Guide speaks of a concrete stepping stone that must be usable, and says that multiple Increments may be created and delivered before the Review.

2The Definition of Done (SF 4.6)

"The Definition of Done is a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product."

Rule Guide wording
Transparency It "creates transparency by providing everyone a shared understanding of what work was completed as part of the Increment"
Not meeting it "If a Product Backlog item does not meet the Definition of Done, it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. Instead, it returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration"
Organizational standard "If the Definition of Done for an increment is part of the standards of the organization, all Scrum Teams must follow it as a minimum"
No organizational standard "The Scrum Team must create a Definition of Done appropriate for the product"
Who conforms "The Developers are required to conform to the Definition of Done"
Multiple teams "If there are multiple Scrum Teams working together on a product, they must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done"
Exam angle

no Definition of Done met, no Increment. An item that is "almost done" is not Done, is not presented and returns to the Product Backlog. The Definition of Done is not lowered to meet a date.

2.1 Who owns it

  • The Developers are required to conform to it and hold each other accountable (Topic 3).
  • The Scrum Team creates it when the organization has no standard; the organization's standard is the minimum that teams extend.
  • The Scrum Master helps the team focus on Increments that meet it; the Product Owner does not relax it for convenience.

3Advantages of a Strong Definition of Done (CSM 1.15)

The objective asks for at least three Beyond the Guide, built on the Guide's statements.

Advantage Why
Transparency and shared understanding Everyone, inside and outside the team, knows what "Done" means (the Guide's own statement)
Built-in quality Quality measures are part of every item, so quality does not decrease
Less rework and fewer defects Problems are caught before an item is called Done
Less technical debt Shortcuts that would pile up are not accepted as Done (Topic 14)
Better forecasting The Guide: the more the Developers know about "their Definition of Done", the more confident they are in their Sprint forecasts
Release readiness A usable Increment can be delivered at any time, "never" waiting for a gate
Trust Stakeholders can rely on what is shown at the Sprint Review
No "almost done" Items are Done or not, which makes progress honest

4Creating a Definition of Done (CSM 1.16)Beyond the Guide

The Guide says who creates it (the Scrum Team, unless the organization has a standard) and that it must fit the product. It gives no method. One workable way, in steps:

Step What to do
1. Collect the organization's standards Regulations, security and compliance policies, architecture standards: these are the minimum
2. Identify the quality the product needs The Scrum Team asks: what must be true of an item before we can safely release it? Typical areas: code and design quality, testing, security, performance, documentation, integration, deployment
3. Brainstorm and select The Scrum Team lists candidate criteria, merges duplicates and keeps those that are verifiable (yes or no) and apply to every item
4. Make it visible and agree Write it down, post it, and make sure every Developer understands and agrees
5. Apply it to every item Plan the work needed to meet it in Sprint Planning
6. Inspect and strengthen Review it in Retrospectives and tighten it as the team learns

Illustrative checklist (a team chooses its own): code reviewed; automated tests pass; no known defects; security checks passed; documentation updated; integrated and deployed to a test environment; non-functional criteria met.

Other starting points: begin from a template and adapt it; start from the defects that escaped in the last Sprints; or start with a small set the team can meet now, and strengthen it each Sprint.

5How the Definition of Done Evolves (SF 4.8)Beyond the Guide

The Guide has the Retrospective inspect "their Definition of Done" and makes the Definition of Done the commitment of the Increment, but it does not describe its evolution. The usual answer:

  • It is a living agreement that is strengthened over time, not relaxed.
  • Triggers: lessons from the Retrospective, defects that escaped, new tooling or automation, new regulations or organizational standards, a growing product, a more skilled team.
  • Effect: it can reveal work missing from previously Done items.
Old wording

The 2017 Guide said: "As Scrum Teams mature, it is expected that their definitions of 'Done' will expand to include more stringent criteria for higher quality. New definitions, as used, may uncover work to be done in previously 'Done' increments." It also said that "any one product or system should have a definition of 'Done' that is a standard for any work done on it". The 2020 Guide no longer says this in words, but the Retrospective still inspects the Definition of Done.

6Multiple Teams, One Definition of Done (SF 4.9)

When several Scrum Teams work on one product, they share the Product Goal, the Product Backlog and the Product Owner (Topic 3) and "must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done".

Reasons (give at least two) Beyond the Guide:

Reason Explanation
One integrated Increment Each Increment must be "additive to all prior Increments" and "thoroughly verified, ensuring that all Increments work together". Work to different standards would not fit together
Consistent quality The product has one quality bar, whichever team built a part
Shared transparency Stakeholders and the Product Owner understand what "Done" means across the whole product
No hidden unfinished work A weaker standard in one team leaves work for later, and creates integration problems
Fair and reliable progress Progress toward the Product Goal is comparable and trustworthy

7Exam Traps and What the Exam Expects

  1. Done means the Definition of Done is met. "Almost done" is not Done.
  2. An item that does not meet it is not presented and not released. It returns to the Product Backlog.
  3. The Developers are required to conform. The Scrum Master and Product Owner do not "relax" it.
  4. Organizational standard first. If it exists, every team follows it as a minimum. Otherwise the Scrum Team creates one.
  5. Several teams on one product share one Definition of Done, defined mutually.
  6. An Increment must be usable. It may be delivered before the Review; the Review is not a gate.
  7. Multiple Increments per Sprint are normal. The sum is presented at the Review.
  8. Quality does not decrease. Lowering the Definition of Done to meet a date is wrong.
  9. The Definition of Done is the commitment of the Increment (not of the Sprint Backlog or the Product Backlog).
  10. No "hardening Sprint". Quality is built into every item through the Definition of Done.
  11. Old wording "Potentially releasable", "Done increment" and the 2017 remark on maturing definitions are old wording. The 2020 term is a usable Increment.

8Exam Q&A

8.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1A Developer finishes an item on day three that meets the Definition of Done. The Product Owner wants to wait until the Sprint Review to release it. What does the Guide say?

  • AThe Sprint Review must approve every release, so no Increment may go to users before the stakeholders accept it at the Review
  • BItems can only be released after the Retrospective, which confirms that the team's way of working was sound
  • CAn Increment may be delivered before the end of the Sprint; the Sprint Review is never a gate to releasing value
  • DThe Scrum Master must approve the release, because the Scrum Master is accountable for Scrum in the team
Show the answer

Answer: C. The moment an item meets the Definition of Done, an Increment is born, and it may be delivered to stakeholders before the end of the Sprint. The Review is for inspection, not for permission.

S2The organization has a security standard that all products must meet. The Scrum Team wants a weaker Definition of Done to move faster. What is the answer?

  • AThe organization's standard is the minimum that all Scrum Teams must follow; the team may add criteria
  • BThe team may ignore it for products that have a low risk, if the Product Owner agrees to the lower quality
  • CThe Product Owner decides which parts of the standard apply, since the Product Owner is accountable for value
  • DThe team may follow it only in the last Sprint before release, when the quality risks are the highest
Show the answer

Answer: A. If the Definition of Done is part of the standards of the organization, all Scrum Teams must follow it as a minimum. A team may extend it with criteria appropriate for its product but may not weaken it.

S3Three Scrum Teams work on one product, each with its own Definition of Done, and integration problems appear every Sprint. What should the Scrum Master advise?

  • ALet each team keep its own and add an integration phase
  • BAsk the Product Owner to choose the strongest team's definition
  • CAdd a hardening Sprint
  • DThe teams must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done
Show the answer

Answer: D. When multiple Scrum Teams work together on a product, they must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done. Each Increment must be thoroughly verified so that all Increments work together.

S4At the end of the Sprint, one item has passed development but not its testing. What happens to it?

  • AIt is presented at the Review as "nearly done", so that the stakeholders can see the progress of the team
  • BIt cannot be released or presented at the Review, and it returns to the Product Backlog
  • CThe Product Owner accepts it as Done, since the Product Owner is accountable for the value of the product
  • DThe Definition of Done is changed for this item, so that the item can be counted as part of the Increment
Show the answer

Answer: B. If a Product Backlog item does not meet the Definition of Done, it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review, and it returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration.

S5How many Increments may a Scrum Team create in one Sprint?

  • AExactly one, at the end of the Sprint
  • BOne per Developer
  • CMultiple Increments may be created within a Sprint
  • DNone until the Review
Show the answer

Answer: C. Multiple Increments may be created within a Sprint, each when an item meets the Definition of Done, and the sum is presented at the Sprint Review.

S6A new team with no organizational standard asks who creates the Definition of Done. What is the best answer?

  • AThe Product Owner alone, because the Product Owner is accountable for the value and the quality of the product
  • BThe Scrum Team creates a Definition of Done appropriate for the product, and the Developers conform to it
  • CThe Scrum Master alone, because the Scrum Master is accountable for establishing Scrum and its quality rules
  • DThe stakeholders, because they know best what quality they expect from every Increment that they see at the Review
Show the answer

Answer: B. If the Definition of Done is not an organizational standard, the Scrum Team must create one appropriate for the product, and the Developers are required to conform to it.

S7Which of the following is an advantage of a strong Definition of Done?

  • AIt gives everyone a shared understanding of what is complete and builds quality into every item
  • BIt removes the need for Retrospectives, because the quality of the work is already checked for each item
  • CIt lets the Scrum Master approve releases, so that no Increment reaches users without a quality check
  • DIt guarantees that Sprints will be shorter, because the Developers no longer spend time on rework
Show the answer

Answer: A. The Definition of Done creates transparency by giving everyone a shared understanding of what work was completed, and it builds quality in. It does not remove the need for inspection and adaptation.

S8In the Retrospective, the team realizes that many defects escape to production. How should the Definition of Done evolve?

  • ALower it to speed up delivery, because the defects show that the team is spending too much time on quality
  • BKeep it unchanged to avoid arguments, because the team agreed to it at the start of the product
  • CLet the Product Owner remove criteria that slow down the team, since the Product Owner orders the work
  • DStrengthen it, for example by adding a criterion that would have caught the defects
Show the answer

Answer: D. The Retrospective inspects the Definition of Done, and the team plans ways to increase quality and effectiveness. As the team learns, its Definition of Done becomes stronger, not weaker.

S9The Product Owner asks to count an item that does not meet the Definition of Done as part of the Increment "just this once" to show progress. What should the Scrum Master say?

  • AAgree, because the Product Owner decides
  • BAgree if the stakeholders accept it
  • CWork cannot be considered part of an Increment unless it meets the Definition of Done
  • DAgree if the Developers are willing to finish it next Sprint
Show the answer

Answer: C. The Guide says work cannot be considered part of an Increment unless it meets the Definition of Done. Making exceptions removes transparency and quality.

S10What must an Increment be in order to provide value?

  • AUsable
  • BApproved by the Product Owner
  • CReleased to customers
  • DDocumented in full
Show the answer

Answer: A. The Guide says that in order to provide value, the Increment must be usable. Release is a separate decision, and approval gates are not in the Guide.

8.2 Recall Q&As

R1What is an Increment?

Show the answer

A concrete stepping stone toward the Product Goal; additive to all prior Increments and thoroughly verified; it must be usable.

R2When is an Increment born?

Show the answer

The moment a Product Backlog item meets the Definition of Done.

R3Can there be several Increments in one Sprint?

Show the answer

Yes. The sum is presented at the Sprint Review.

R4Is the Sprint Review a gate to release?

Show the answer

No. An Increment may be delivered to stakeholders before the end of the Sprint.

R5What is the Definition of Done?

Show the answer

A formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product; the commitment of the Increment.

R6What does the Definition of Done create?

Show the answer

Transparency: a shared understanding of what work was completed.

R7What happens to an item that does not meet it?

Show the answer

It cannot be released or presented at the Sprint Review; it returns to the Product Backlog.

R8If the organization has a standard Definition of Done?

Show the answer

All Scrum Teams must follow it as a minimum.

R9If there is no organizational standard?

Show the answer

The Scrum Team creates a Definition of Done appropriate for the product.

R10Who is required to conform to it?

Show the answer

The Developers.

R11What applies to Scrum Teams on one product?

Show the answer

They must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done.

R12Name three advantages of a strong Definition of Done.

Show the answer

Shared understanding and transparency; built-in quality; less rework and technical debt; better forecasts; release readiness; trust.

R13Give one way to create a Definition of Done.

Show the answer

Start from the organization's standards as the minimum; the Scrum Team brainstorms and selects verifiable quality criteria for the product; apply them to every item; strengthen them in Retrospectives.

R14How does a Definition of Done evolve?

Show the answer

It is strengthened over time through Retrospective learning, new tooling and standards; it is not relaxed.

9Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Increment Concrete stepping stone toward the Product Goal; additive; thoroughly verified; usable
Born when An item meets the Definition of Done
Multiple Several per Sprint; the sum is shown at the Review; may be delivered earlier
Review Never a gate to releasing value
Definition of Done The commitment of the Increment; formal description of quality measures met
Transparency A shared understanding of what was completed
Not met Not released, not presented; back to the Product Backlog
Organization standard Minimum for all Scrum Teams; otherwise the Scrum Team creates one
Conform The Developers
Several teams, one product The same, mutually defined Definition of Done
Strong DoD gives Transparency · quality · less rework and debt · confident forecasts · release readiness
Evolves Stronger over time through Retrospectives; never lowered for a date
Old wording "Potentially releasable", "Done increment" (2017)
